Let that prophetic saying never be uttered of you: Their daughters adorned, decked round about like the likeness of a temple, and whitened outside like tombs, which shine outwardly with gold but inside are most foul and unclean, full of the corpses of the dead. Such are daughters not of Christ the king, but of Tyre. These, always about gifts, these by the shamelessness of their faces, are captured by the rich of the people and capture them. Most imperfect is the disposition of women. Always in clothes, always in gold, precious stones and outward ornaments do they place their glory. The lust innate in nature is not enough for them, but they seek occasions to satisfy lust. Without doubt they aim that the eyes of men, contemplating the gold and gems, may at last be fixed on the face, so that with the nods of their eyes they may more easily incite them to the fire of lust. Why, common harlot, do you glory in pearls and gems? What do silver and gold have to do with you? Why are you exalted in the beauty of cloth? Is not all flesh ash and hay, and to speak more truly, a mass of rottenness, food of worms and most stinking dung? What in you is to be admired, what to be praised, spectacle for boys? Even if the preciousness of the gems and metals, which nature gave them, is praised, yet you are always known as ash, hay, and unclean dung produced from unclean seed. O if you would look at yourself, most vile of women, how ashamed you would be of the body which you cultivate with such care! For you are either equal to the beast of burden and the beasts of the earth, or worse: within is that in which you should glory, not without. In this so foul vessel you hold a treasure which you ought to cultivate with the greatest diligence and keep with the greatest watchfulness. It matters nothing to you about the earthen vessel, if its form outside is foul, so long as what lies hidden within is noble, within is beautiful, what is kept within is intact.
CHAPTER XXIX.
On the danger of ambition for garments.

Therefore you, dearest ones, who are brides and daughters of the eternal king, whose kingdom will not be corrupted nor taken from him, let all your glory be from within. Sit at the right hand of the bridegroom in clothing not outer but inner, gilded with the gold of charity in golden fringes, that is, the precepts of charity; let the garment be surrounded on every side with varieties, so that nothing of the virtues may be lacking in the ornaments. Let there be myrrh, stacte and cassia from the garments, so that in the odour of virtues and of life the other young maidens may run from the world to your holiness. Delight in this honour of yours, daughters of the eternal king. This beauty of yours your king and bridegroom will desire. So you will remain with him in the bridal chamber in gladness and exultation. Then sons will be born of you who will fill not the earth but heaven, whom the Father will make princes over all the earth.

But if ambition for outer garments delighted you, if, having gone out from the pomp of the world, from the house of the devil, and from the congregation of the wicked, you had not totally forgotten your people and your father's house, exalting yourselves either in the dignities of your parents, or in the lineage of the flesh, or in such most perishable vanities, vapours of the earth, as is customary for the inhabitants of the earth, at once the most mighty king, rising, girt upon his thigh with a two-edged sword, will drive you out from his tabernacle with his right hand, wounded on every side. Then his most sharp arrows will pierce your hearts in bitterness, since the rod of his kingdom is a rod of uprightness. And afterwards, when you are cast out of the house of your Lord, all will mock you and will say of each of you: Wretched daughter of Babylon, who did not make God your helper but hoped in your vanity: sit now by the rivers of Babylon; lament, and hang your instruments on the willows, while you remember whence you were expelled. For you who used to sing the song of praise and gladness now weep, led away into a foreign land.
CHAPTER XXX.
On the consideration of the last day of judgement.

Therefore, dearest ladies, with the Apostle consider yourselves in this world as dung and the refuse of the world, so that you may please your bridegroom. Nothing of the pomps of the world pertains to you, who renounced in baptism the world, the devil and their pomps; which you also afterwards confirmed under the promise of an oath at your entry into religion. Let no talk ever be held among you of nobility of family or lineage of the flesh. Let the daughter of a king or of a peasant be equal in the service of God. All together you have one nobility and dignity from the bridegroom. Go out continually outside the camp with Christ, so that with Christ you may be crucified to the world and to vices, bearing reproaches with him; and for love of him let the labour of the duties of the house seem sweet.

Let there be no dispute about the greater importance of offices, but about devotion and eagerness in carrying them out. Let no murmuring, no sound of foul words, no sound of quarrels ever be heard among those dead to the world. Buried corpses never carry on quarrels among themselves in their tombs, never blaspheme, never contend: so also you, dearest ones, lulled in the sleep of quiet and peace, should await your bridegroom and judge; should await the great and terrible day of judgement, that is, the day of wrath, the day of calamity, when heaven together with earth will tremble, all the powers of the heavens will be moved, the angels will be trembling together with all the saints; then the perils of each one's life will be examined, and merits will appear. Let that terrible trumpet always resound in your ears: Rise, you dead, come to judgement. Behold, the king comes with a mighty hand; he wishes to demand an account from all, surely of the smallest thoughts, surely of light and idle words. If you are not ready to render an account of each thing, you will be cast into the outer prison; you will hear from the judge: Go, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.
CHAPTER XXXI.
On seeking out lowliness in clothing.

Alas, most unhappy heart, most unfortunate mind, which does not meditate daily on so dreadful a day of judgement; and if it does meditate on it, it is most foolish if it desires anything of the world and its pomps. Let all these things pass you by on no day, at no hour. Let every wall of the house, every corner, be shown before your eyes painted with that day. If this lesson is not neglected, then the lowliness of clothing, which wearies foolish little women, will delight you. Then rustic and lowly cloth will be preferred to purple and fine linen. Then coarse and rough head-veils will be valued as if [they were] of silk. Surely there will be such ugliness in the sheepskins, such coarseness in the cowls, hoods prepared with such rough workmanship, that if such were the garments of people in the world, all the industry of the cloth-makers would perish in a short time.

These things, dearest ones, befit nuns: not, with tight sleeves, precious and elaborate cloths, and brows veiled with fine veiling, to have the heart of harlots even more than to display it. I do not consider such women nuns, but the worst harlots and the vilest whores. For the corpses of the dead have no need of precious and elaborate ornaments in their tombs. Tombs do not need such things; the stones of the monastery do not seek the glory of clothes, which can by no means be had without great sin. Soft things are to be left to the actors and entertainers of the kings and princes of the world. It is John's part to be clothed with camels' hair. Let one be ashamed, then, to have the name of religion and to show oneself an actor by the adornment of clothes. And therefore, dearest ones, I wish you, dead to the world, who have wholly trampled on the world, to go about in such ugly and unkempt clothing that, if shameless eyes were permitted to look upon you, laughter rather than evil thought would be provoked. I declare indeed that those lie who boast that they keep chastity and yet pursue wantonness in their clothes. So let your cloth, even if white and bright, nevertheless be coarse and cheap, so that the colour may display the inward brightness of chastity, and the uniformity the contempt of earthly things. This is the glory of nuns; this the course of religious minds; this the mark of the brides of the eternal God; this the sign of those dead to the world and buried with Christ.
CHAPTER XXXII.
On seeking out austerity in bedding.

Let married women and widows who remain in the world be anxious about many things, about laborious things; occupied daily with frequent service, let them be saved with Martha through works of piety, ministering to Jesus in the poor; let them break their bread for the hungry; let them bring the needy and wanderers into their house; let them clothe the naked, let them persevere in works of mercy, works without doubt so fruitful and good that it is impossible that they should not appease God when angered. Let them loose the bonds of wickedness, undoing the bundles, and break every burden.

But you, dearest ones, who with Mary have chosen the better, indeed the best, part, sit continually at the feet of Jesus, turning over the volumes of the sacred Scriptures in sacred readings. Wash his feet with constant tears of compunction and joy, of charity and devotion, intent on the sweetness of contemplation. Wipe them with your hair, expelling through it from your heart the superfluity of all earthly things. Hear from the mouth of Jesus the word that passes through hearts like a two-edged sword, cutting the joints of the limbs even to the division of the spirit. This word will be sweet to your throats beyond honey and the honeycomb. [This is] the word through which all things were made; this the word which the devotion of the centurion asked for, that his servant might be healed. Only those who hear it know the sweetness of this word. Those who are sleepy and given to sloth cannot hear this word.

Therefore, dearest ones, I wish you each night to lie in your little cells on a short and hard bed: not on feathers and soft things, but either on chaff or straw, or rather in wooden boxes than in beds, so that the tamed limbs may shrink from the bed rather than long for it; so that necessity rather than desire may compel the rest of approaching sleep. Thus, because of the hardness, let a short and light sleep take hold, so that the sleeping mind may not be tormented by the usual illusions of the night.
CHAPTER XXXIII.
On Matins and the manner of saying the divine office.

Let midnight prepare you for the vigils of Matins. Let the summons of the bell find none of you asleep. Let it not be unknown whether [a delay] was from sleep, but rather [let it be] from the ecstasy of contemplation. Having first prayed in your little cells, let each of the sisters come to the church in the deepest quiet of midnight and rouse the beloved bridegroom with the praises of Matins, so that he may rise to their help. Let the psalms and sacred readings be delivered so distinctly and alternately that the angelic spirits are not provoked to laughter by clashing sounds, gaps and barbarisms. Let the sound of the voices always be so moderate, attentive, quiet and sweet that no pomp and no carnal delight has place in the divine praises: let the highest devotion pour out frequent sighs and tears.

Let such slowness and such speed be kept in the manner that neither weariness nor stumbling of the tongue can arise. Let no words, however very useful, ever be uttered among those chanting the psalms; but let that which is treated outwardly be ruminated inwardly in the secret of the mind with the greatest diligence. It is of no merit to pray the divine offices with wordiness, and with a wretched mind to wander around the things that press from outside. When the morning praises are finished, let sleep not seize you even then, lest it be scattered what the bridegroom answers to the petitions of his brides. Soon, in chapter, to the attentive and devout sisters let a devout reading of the holy books reveal from the will of their Lord whatever is to be done. And thus let the illusions and phantoms of demons, which would mock them as they slept, give way. Immediately let another very short reading follow the reading, on the things which pertain to instruction in the apostolic life, treated in whatever style in the present little work, so that thus each day the pious mind, fed as if by a morsel, may desire sweetness, and not be held back by weariness, and may think of excellent things from small ones. After the readings let there follow confessions of faults in the regular disciplines before the abbess of the house and the other sisters.

Let whatever has been done against the regular observances and obediences be brought out in public, so that nothing at all may now pass uncorrected and unpunished, and the condition of each may not be hidden from the mother and the sisters; so that, both through shame and through the discipline which the mother imposes, each may be made wary for the time to come. But to utter anything of these things outside the chapter, by any word or nod, let it be anathema. With this end let the holy enclosed [assembly] depart.
CHAPTER XXXIV.
On the order of saying the hours of Prime, Terce, Sext and None.

Let the saving day begin with the praises of Prime; when these are finished, let the mysteries of the sacred Mass, because of the bridegroom's presence, gladden the hearts of the brides, inebriate them with the drink of charity, and satisfy them with the food of devotion and faith at the saving banquet. Afterwards let each one have opportunity either to pray, or to read the sacred volumes, or otherwise to do holy works. Then let the learned instruct the little novice girls on the evangelical life, holy conduct, the duties of the house and the regular disciplines, until the hour of the meal. Meanwhile let the food also be prepared, by which bodies may be refreshed for the yoke of penance.

Let the mind never be given to idleness, lest at any time thoughts and impulses tickle minds with illicit things; and if in any way they begin to rise up, let them be crushed at once in the seed, lest tares grow with the wheat: let whatever is wrongly conceived vanish through labours or works of the hands. Let [the sister] go to a holy sister, so that what is unclean may be cast out by holy conversation. It is very safe to have a faithful and just friend, to whom whatever lies hidden in the secret bosom of the heart may be laid open at once. For a person often cannot have right judgement in his own affairs.

When the hour of the meal comes, at which nature compels one to pay the body its due, on ordinary days let the praises of the hours of Terce and Sext first be devoutly rendered to God. Afterwards, with all modesty, the blessing having first been given by the abbess, let them take food, and let a part serve. After the others have eaten, let those who had served also eat, and be served by others. But when a time of fasting has made the meal later, let the sacred mysteries of the Mass, Terce, Sext and None come first; on other days let None be said after the meal at the appointed hour, when the sun in the middle of its circuit shows midday.
CHAPTER XXXV.
On food and the order of eating.

For when the due hour has gathered you for the meal, let the industry of cooks by no means shine in your food. Let not the nobility of the dishes move the appetite, but hunger; let not incitements to lust be served, but things that can quench hunger: let either pulses or vegetables be seasoned with oil. Let meat be granted only by licence of the abbess to the weak and sick; otherwise let the community not know what it tastes like. Let eggs and milk foods be permitted as a favour to sisters weakened after fasts and on principal feasts.

Let the things that arise and live in the waters be known rarely, except little fishes. Let the horrid crime of gluttony, mother of lust and executioner of chastity, have no share with the handmaids of God. Therefore let there be such sobriety in eating, such fitting frugality, that the belly is constrained rather than gratified. Let the stomach not need medicines for digestion: let emptiness rather than excessive fullness bring on belching. Nor let there be need to let out the belt, so that the mind may not be held back from meditations on God by surfeit, and the body may not need medicines. Let eating always be ordered and composed in its manner. Let there not be such speed of the throat in taking a dish, and such quick chewing of the morsel, that some suspicion of greed might rightly arise. In eating, it is not so much the food as an unseemly manner that is to be blamed. For often, over beans and barley bread, excessive greed causes great sin. Let the greedy and wandering eyes by no means roam here and there over those reclining at table and note this one or that one eating more or less. Let the number of those dining not occupy the mind of anyone.
CHAPTER XXXVI.
On sobriety and fasting.

Wine too, in which there is wantonness, should be suspect to the brides of Christ as a poison. Let weakness of the stomach and the debility of an afflicted nature decide its use, rather than pleasure or greed. But if necessity itself all but compels it to be taken, then let the wine be served for drinking either so weak or so mixed with water that the head is by no means filled with fumes and pours out ridiculous or childish words. Drunkenness is reckoned a sacrilege, in a woman especially, but infinitely more in a bride of the Lord. Let the uncovering of Noah's private parts, and Lot's incest, brought about by drunkenness, make you cautious, and render you always fearful and always wary. Believe truly that whoever constantly uses wine carries fire in her lap.

I beg you, among women dead to the body, who have renounced all pleasures for Christ, let not even the slightest word be spoken of the horrid crime of gluttony and the filth of drunkenness. Gluttony of the belly and drunkenness furnish the cause and matter of infirmity of the soul as much as of the body. Therefore let medicinal fasting take away all languor and bestow all virtue and grace. Let the lawgiver teach you this, to whom the law is not given before the forty days' fast is completed. Elijah, in the strength of bread baked in the ashes, went fasting for forty days to Horeb, the Mountain of God. What virtue holy fasting contains, learn from your bridegroom, who, having completed a fast of forty days, overcame the temptation of the devil. Let the men of Nineveh not be passed over in silence, who by fasting escaped the common destruction and changed the irrevocable sentence of God. Imitate these, dearest ones, but follow them wisely, lest it be said by the Lord: This is not the fast that I have chosen.

Chastise your members, but do not kill them. Let fasting not cause shame, so as to be a scandal to others; let the sacred readings not be omitted through headache and weakness of body, nor prayers fail, lest it be necessary to abandon contemplation. Let each apply to herself through fasting the medicine for her own health. Let the body be broken by fasts; let the handmaid be chastised with blows. If it desires anything unlawful, let abstinences be multiplied and the heaviest disciplines applied, until it becomes so humble, so kindly, that it claims nothing harmful for itself and demands nothing you do not want. Let the mistress be raised up and rule in all things; let the handmaid be made subject, put underfoot and trampled. But if again and again she raises herself against the mistress, let the handmaid be cast out, stripped, wearied and humbled as you wish. But if you choose to harass a quiet body beyond its strength and beyond what is fitting, it will grow indignant and throw you into the pit of indiscretion. For nothing that indiscretion does, that imprudence imposes, and that lack of foresight teaches can have any virtue.
CHAPTER XXXVII.
On readings at table.

So sweet are the words of the Lord to a healthy palate that, once tasted, they never cloy. Through their sweetness and pleasantness they always generate new appetites. It befits you always to taste them. At no time ever are you to cease from prayer. The Apostle instructs you to pray always, you who are not bound, like married women, to be free for a time [from prayer] for the allurements of the flesh. Therefore pray always as far as you can, and while the body is fed with food, let the soul be filled with reading. It is not right even for people of the world to take food and at the same time belch out empty words.

Let the sister appointed for each week read to those eating a holy reading from the Old Testament and from the New, and from the deeds and sayings of the saints. Then let each one's sober mind be intent on the sweetness of the word of God; let it sigh anxiously when the prophetic or historical word shows God's severity toward the wicked. Let it be filled with immense joy when God's kindness toward the good is announced. Let hope revive when it is shown by promise or by deed that indulgence can be granted to penitents. Let faith be raised up when God is shown faithful in his promises. Let charity be kindled when our humanity is endowed with so many privileges and gifts from the birth of Christ, from his life and passion and resurrection, and our lowliness is exalted. Let not words resound, but sighs; not laughter and guffaws, but tears. Let hands not be occupied with useless cuttings, but let breasts be beaten at the remembrance of sins. For, driven by these reins, the savage rapacity of the gullet does not exceed the limits of sobriety; surfeit will not be at the doors of the belly; and finally, burning lust will do no harm.
CHAPTER XXXVIII.
On the work of the sisters after the midday meal

When the food has been taken, let not even then gossip be resorted to, but, after the example of Christ, let them rise with the praises of God to give thanks, and render hymns to God in the church. Then, in all silence, so that the holy reading that was read may profit and what was recounted may be written on the mind, let each one individually go over it again and fix it, or meditate in the church on what she has learned, until on ordinary days, after the midday meal, they have celebrated together the fitting praises of the hour of None in the church; or if perhaps on fast days the hour of None comes before the meal, until the little bell is rung in the cloister. Meanwhile, if the shortness of the nights, the condition of the season and the need of nature require it, after some short hour in which there is to be reading or prayer after the meal, let those who wish be allowed for a little while to refresh the body with rest rather than sleep, so that it may be restored strong for labours.

After the rest, when the hour of None is over or the little bell has been rung, so that the devil may find nothing idle and the entrance of the heart may not lie open to vain desires, let one of the sisters copy books, so that both the hand may be filled with labour and the mind with divine food. Let another sew the sisters' cowls, tunics and sheepskins. Let another plant vegetable seedlings in the little garden, so that as they grow they may provide you with food. Let another sow seeds. Let the beds be watered, so that they become fit for the seeds. Let fruit-bearing trees be grafted onto barren ones, so that art may overcome the force of nature. From these things let the mind rise, through looking at these visible things, to meditate on the invisible things of God; let wonder arise at the divine power in the seed, that from something so small and so dry a creature of such size, greenness and beauty is formed. From wonder let devotion grow, from devotion the lifting up of the mind, so that the little garden itself becomes an oratory, and insensible creatures proclaim the greatness of the Creator. But above all care must be taken that your hands dare not touch anything that could be fitted to vain uses.
CHAPTER XXXIX.
On the evening hours, and Compline.

Serpent of morals, let all idle talk be expelled from your midst. Let laughter never, guffaws never proclaim a vain heart. Let all the actions of the body be so holy, so modest, that they display the holiness of the mind. For the outer man is the index of the inner. Let the evening hour find you warring down the devil in holy labour, in holy work; at which hour let God be praised in the church with holy offices.

If the solemnity of a feast, or excessive weakness, has granted a common little supper and a brief refreshment of the body prepared rather [for need] than for pleasure, let the evening praises be rendered to God earlier than on other fast days, so that the praises due in the last hour of the day are not omitted or in any way cut short because of the supper. When the supper is finished, or, if it is omitted, after some short hour according to the needs of the season, let the little bell call the sisters to the church, where a devout reading is to be given either from the deeds of the saints or from other wonders of God. Let the praises of Compline follow it, so that minds strengthened by this divine food may not dread to meet the phantoms of the night and the hidden deceits of the devil, nor fear to fight; and thus the day that began with divine services may end in divine praises.

After Compline let nothing be heard but silence, so that the sisters, at rest and wholly withdrawn from the bodily senses, may ruminate in their minds and hold fast in their hearts what they heard earlier in the divine readings. Meditating on these things, let each go to her little cell, having received the mother's blessing, and wearing the habit of religion, so that, if nature requires, she may lay herself on her bed to rest. But if the demon, who had feared her awake, begins to pursue her asleep, if he sends illusions, if he sets foul things before her thought, as soon as the bride of God perceives it, let her rise, and let sloth and sleep give way to swift watchfulness. Then at once let her set against the devil the sign of the cross, horrible and terrifying to him, let her call on the help of her beloved bridegroom, and the jealous bridegroom, who guards his bride with great zeal, will at once rise up to the help of his bride. He will surround her with a shield, so that she will no longer fear the terror of the night. And at once a thousand will fall at her side, and ten thousand at her right hand, and they will not come near her. Lastly, he will command his angels to guard her in all her ways, lest perhaps she strike her foot against a stone.
CHAPTER XL.
On keeping charity toward sick sisters.

Let the flesh of a bride of God not take up the softness of baths. Their use does not suit chaste bodies. We ourselves, from daily experience, feel well enough how great a fire of lust burns in our members, even if the fuel of the fire is removed as far as possible. Too mad and foolish is he who, preparing material for fire to burn, does not want it to burn. These things befit wretched little women when they are endangered by the shipwreck of childbirth. Yet if extreme necessity has counselled it for a sick woman, let it be done with all modesty, the honour of all chastity being preserved. Otherwise let it be unlawful for the servants of God to think of such things. Let it be kept with the greatest care among you that toward sick sisters, with all solicitude, every care of hospitality is shown, and services of complete and entire kindness are provided. If danger requires it, let them at once consult a physician who is sober and chaste and free from all suspicion; and whatever he prescribes as suited to health, let it be done kindly, setting aside every need of the house. But if necessities are lacking, let the things of the monastery be sold, so that nothing temporal may hinder works of mercy.

Let no law of food, drink or bedding bind a sick or weak sister. Yet care must be taken that the craving of gluttony does not seek its own comfort under the veil of sickness, and that sickness, under the appearance of holiness, does not wear down the body with abstinences beyond its strength, lest the body, broken by a double goad and failing before the just Judge, accuse the community of impiety and of murder. Let discreet and holy sisters be appointed as keepers for the sick, who will carefully guard against the dangers that can threaten the sick, so that nothing adverse may happen in any way. Let the serving women not, I beg, find their burdens heavy. Let them always think of Christ hidden in the sick sister; let them always think that they may come to need such things in the future. Let that law of nature always be held bound in the bosom of the mind, that a person ought to show to others what he would himself ask of them. Let murmuring not, I beg, taint the works of hospitality, but let what ought to be done be done with all gentleness, according to the Apostle, who says: Pursuing hospitality, [bearing with] one another in charity without murmuring.
CHAPTER XLI.
On the authority of the bishop and the provost concerning the observances of the order.

See, my lady Eustochium, and the rest of you most beloved daughters of Christ: an old father, already near to death, being a hundred years in age, has sent you with devoted affection the apostolic life, written on these little pages in a rough and coarse style. In this mirror, as in a riddle in the present life, let each one of the daughters discern by constant meditation the way of eternal happiness. Let the coarseness of the bark not cause contempt for seeking out the pith. Let unskilled and rustic speech not breed disgust. Such things befit poetic fables. A work of piety and of all truth has no need to be read with the pomp of rhetoricians. All these things belong to the young. From this, each day, as from a delightful dish, take for yourselves a morsel of each. Do not swallow it down, but chewing it with great slowness, move it this way and that in your mouth, so that you may be able to taste its sweetness. For I confess to you that from the things written here, if meditation is diligent, such things will rise up for you as human tongue has not known, although this too is an imperfect work. For no constitution is so holy, so just and so long considered that it will not suffer very many defects in the future, or will not at some time need correction. Therefore, if anything in this little rule of the apostolic life and of religion needs dispensation, correction or change, I commit it to your bishop or to your holy provost priest, that he may dispense, change and correct according to the fullness of the Holy Spirit. So then, dearest daughters, live holy days. So [live], joined to Christ by the marriage covenant, that when the bridegroom comes in the middle of the night to call you to the wedding, he may find you always ready, not with an empty lamp, and not seeking oil for yourselves outside, lest, as with the foolish [virgins], entry to the bridal chamber be denied you because of your lateness. Help the old age of your devoted Jerome with your holy prayers.
